title: Classical Cellular Automaton for Measurement-Only Entanglement Transitions
authors: Will Holdhusen, Bailey Mae McAmis, Armin Rahmani
abstract: We introduce a generalized classical long-range stochastic cellular automaton that exactly captures the entanglement dynamics and transitions of a measurement-only monitored quantum system. The corresponding quantum model consists of a one-dimensional qubit chain subject to competing single-site and long-range Bell measurements, with separations drawn from a power-law distribution. At every step of each trajectory, the state remains a tensor product of Bell pairs and unpaired qubits, with bipartite entanglement entropy fully encoded in a classical matching of the sites. This exact representation allows us to solve the dynamics analytically in several limits and to determine the steady-state scaling of the entanglement entropy. We find volume-law, fractal, and area-law regimes. Numerical results show that these regimes persist beyond the analytically solvable limit. Because Bell outcomes affect only Bell-state labels and not the matching, all subsystem entropies are outcome independent, avoiding the exponential cost of trajectory postselection.
summary: This paper develops a novel framework by mapping the complex entanglement dynamics of a measured qubit chain onto a simple classical stochastic cellular automaton. By analyzing this classical model, the authors analytically determine the steady-state scaling of entanglement entropy, revealing distinct volume-law, fractal, and area-law regimes controlled by the measurement parameters. This provides deep insight into how measurement processes govern quantum correlations.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of analytically capturing and solving the entanglement dynamics and transitions in a quantum system monitored only by local measurements.
main_result: The entanglement structure is exactly mapped onto a classical stochastic cellular automaton, allowing the determination of steady-state entanglement scaling laws (volume-law, fractal, and area-law) based on the measurement process parameters.
method: The authors use a mapping technique to translate quantum entanglement dynamics into a classical stochastic process (a matching problem), enabling analytical solutions in specific limits and extensive numerical simulations.
model_or_system: The system is a one-dimensional qubit chain subjected to competing single-site and long-range Bell measurements, where the entanglement state is tracked by a classical matching of the sites.
key_observables: Bipartite entanglement entropy ($S_A(N_A)$), fraction of unentangled sites ($n_1(t)$), and the entanglement scaling exponent ($ eta$).
important_parameters: Measurement probability ($p$), power-law exponent ($\alpha$) governing pair selection, and the system size ($N$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the entanglement dynamics can be exactly represented by a classical stochastic cellular automaton, which avoids the computational cost of trajectory postselection.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the automaton's elementary moves, the entanglement phase diagram showing volume-, fractal-, and area-law regimes, and time evolution plots comparing theoretical scaling predictions with numerical results.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the classical automaton mapping to deriving analytical solutions for specific limits ($\alpha=0$, $p 	o 1^-$), establishing the scaling laws based on $\alpha$, and finally analyzing the time evolution of the transition points between these regimes.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, non-Hamiltonian framework to study entanglement decay and steady-state properties in open quantum systems, which is highly relevant for understanding decoherence and measurement backaction in quantum information processing.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Elementary moves of the stochastic cellular automaton. Red links and meter symbols indicate Bell measurements, while blue arcs denote Bell pairs. (a) Measuring an unpaired qubit and one member of a Bell pair replaces the original pair and leaves its former partner unpaired. (b) Measuring one qubit from each of two Bell pairs pro- duces entanglement swapping, reconnecting their former partners.

FIG. 2. Top: analytically derived entanglement phase diagram in the dilute-pair (p →1−) limit. Bottom: phase diagram for p > 0 obtained from simulations. Heatmap color indicates entropy scaling exponent β where S ∼Nβ. The limit of p = 0 is challenging to study numerically, but analytical results in the α →∞limit give logarith- mic entanglement scaling. At p = 1, the model is fully unentangled and is therefore trivially area law.

FIG. 3. Measured and input pair distributions at α = 0.5 for a 400- qubit system averaged over 105 trials. These results indicate good agreement between input and measured distributions in the dilute limit (p = 0.95). When p is reduced to 0.05, entanglement swap- ping increases the tail of the distribution.

FIG. 4. Half-chain entropy as a function of time in a system with N = 1000 and unentangling measurement rate p = 0.5 averaged over 105 trials. Inset: density of unpaired qubits as a function of time for the same parameters.

FIG. 5. Log-log plots of S A(N/2) obtained from simulations with p = 0.95 averaged over 105 trials. Dashed lines correspond to least- squares fits to a power law ANβ. Error bars (not visible for most points due to their small size) correspond to the standard error of the mean (SEM) from these trials.
